paras: The lynching of John Moore took place early on Sunday, August 27, 1905, when a masked crowd took Moore, a young Black man, from the Craven County jail at New Bern, North Carolina, hanged him from the Neuse River bridge and riddled his body with bullets. Moore had been accused two days earlier of striking a white storekeeper's wife with a meat axe during an attempted robbery. Papers across the country blamed the lynching on the $300 bond set at his hearing, and Governor Glenn ordered the lynchers prosecuted.

According to the New Bern Journal, Moore entered George T. Eubanks's store at Clarks, about seven miles from New Bern, on the morning of Friday, August 25, demanded money from Mrs. Eubanks, and struck her with a meat axe when she refused, fracturing her skull and jaw. Pursuers caught him in a swamp that afternoon; Eubanks reportedly declined to shoot him although neighbors urged it, and brought him to the New Bern jail. Moore protested his innocence, and at a preliminary hearing on Saturday Justice Barrington fixed his bond at $300.

Farmers from the Clarks neighborhood, joined by some New Bern men, arrived about midnight and moved after one o'clock, according to the News and Observer's New Bern correspondent. Sheriff J. W. W. Biddle went into the street to stop them and was held at revolver point and told, "if you go a step further we will kill you." The men then took the keys from Jailer Williams at gunpoint and removed Moore.

The fire bell filled the streets with people, and the Naval Reserves and a cutter crew were summoned, but too late. With his hands tied, Moore was hauled up Craven Street to the draw of the Neuse River bridge, hanged from an iron cross piece and shot at least fifteen times, after which the crowd dispersed quietly.

A coroner's jury found that Moore died of gunshot wounds "at the hands of persons unknown to the jury," since his neck was not broken. Described as a stranger who had worked at a local saw mill, he was buried at county expense, while Mrs. Eubanks was reported likely to recover but disfigured.

Ministers denounced the lynching from New Bern pulpits that morning, and some residents blamed the sheriff for leaving the jail unguarded. Governor Glenn instructed Solicitor L. I. Moore to investigate and prosecute, calling the affair "a blot on North Carolina." By September 7 one man had been arrested, and a federal prisoner held in the jail that night was moved to Goldsboro for questioning; no later report of an indictment or trial appears in the coverage.

The Associated Press story ran on August 28 from New Haven and New York to St. Louis and Montgomery, under headlines such as "Masked Mob Lynches Newberne, N. C., Negro." A Charlotte Observer special printed with it said "the real cause of the lynching" was the low bond, and briefs reached Honolulu, Vermont and Wyoming within days.

Southern headlines leaned toward approval: the Montgomery Advertiser wrote that Moore "Will Not Commit Another Such Deed in Future," and the Semi-Weekly Messenger credited "an Orderly Crowd." The Raleigh News and Observer, reprinted in Monroe and Clinton, called the event deplorable but said "the generalship was perfect" and found local opinion "mostly commendatory of the mob's work." It and a Charlotte dispatch claimed that Black men interviewed approved the lynching, a claim no Black source in the coverage confirms or answers.

Editorials in Clarksburg, West Virginia, and San Antonio disclaimed lynching but blamed the official who set the bond. Glenn's condemnation was reprinted in Washington and, misattributed to the solicitor, in Clarksburg.

The AP and the Goldsboro Argus counted about one hundred masked men; the Evening Star said about fifty farmers, and the News and Observer no more than fifty at the jail. The Goldsboro Argus said the reserves were called only after the lynching, on a rumor of a second one, and the Evening Star placed the assault at the Clark post office rather than the store.

reader.title: Lynching of John Moore
bases: A masked crowd took John Moore from the Craven County jail by force and hanged and shot him (A2, A3, A15).

Moore was killed by a crowd variously numbered at fifty to one hundred that forced the jail without any legal authority (A3, A4, A15); the papers say the mob acted because it thought his $300 bond too light for the assault he was accused of (A2, A15).

The AP dispatch (A3), the Charlotte Observer special (A2, A7), the separate Evening Star account (A4) and the News and Observer's New Bern special (A15) agree on the seizure, hanging and shooting, and a coroner's jury returned a verdict (A16).

accounts.label: AP wire report
accounts.gist: One hundred masked men forced the jail between 1 and 2 a.m., the naval reserves were called out but failed, and Sheriff Biddle pleaded in vain before Moore was hanged from the bridge and shot.

accounts.label: Charlotte Observer special
accounts.gist: The real cause of the lynching was that Moore's bond had been fixed at only $300; the lynching was denounced from the pulpits.

accounts.label: Evening Star account
accounts.gist: About fifty farmers from Clark, angry at the light bond, stopped the sheriff at pistol point and forced Jailer Williams to give up Moore; the assault took place at the Clark post office.

accounts.label: News and Observer New Bern special
accounts.gist: Mostly countrymen with some townsmen, no more than fifty at the jail, took Moore quietly and 'the generalship was perfect'; the reserves were too late; the coroner found death by gunshot.

accounts.label: Goldsboro Argus account
accounts.gist: About one hundred masked men; the sheriff was held back by revolvers; the naval reserves were asked for only after the lynching, on a rumor that another prisoner would be taken.

framing.detail: Northern and Western dailies ran the AP story under headlines such as 'Negro Lynched by Mob' and 'Masked Mob Lynches Newberne, N. C., Negro', foregrounding 'The Negro's Shocking Crime'.

The Montgomery Advertiser headlined that Moore 'Will Not Commit Another Such Deed in Future', and the Semi-Weekly Messenger said he 'Pays the Death Penalty for His Crime' at the hands of 'an Orderly Crowd'.
The Raleigh News and Observer called the event 'deplorable' yet praised the mob's quiet 'generalship', reported local opinion as mostly favorable and claimed Black men approved.
Editorials in Clarksburg and San Antonio disclaimed lynching but blamed the official who set the $300 bond.
Governor Glenn's statement calling it 'a blot on North Carolina' was printed in Washington and Clarksburg.
